Frequently Asked Question: How is porcelain tile different from ceramic tile?
Answer: Porcelain tile and ceramic tile may look similar, but there are some key differences between them. Here's how porcelain tile differs from ceramic tile: Composition: Porcelain tile is made of fine porcelain clay and is fired at a higher temperature than ceramic tile. This makes it denser, harder, and less porous compared to ceramic tile. Durability: Porcelain tile is highly durable and resistant to wear, scratches, and stains. It is suitable for high-traffic areas and is known for its longevity. Ceramic tile is less durable and more prone to chipping and cracking. Water Absorption: Porcelain tile has a lower water absorption rate, usually less than 0.5%. It is considered impervious or vitreous, making it suitable for areas with high moisture, such as bathrooms and kitchens. Ceramic tile has a higher water absorption rate, typically above 0.5%. Versatility: Porcelain tile can be used both indoors and outdoors, thanks to its low water absorption and frost resistance. It is also available in a wide range of finishes, including polished, matte, and textured. Ceramic tile is primarily recommended for indoor use. Maintenance: Due to its low porosity, porcelain tile is easier to clean and maintain. It is less likely to absorb stains or harbor bacteria. Ceramic tile may require more frequent cleaning and sealing to prevent staining and moisture penetration. Price: Porcelain tile is generally more expensive than ceramic tile due to its higher quality and durability. Ceramic tile is often a more budget-friendly option. When choosing between porcelain and ceramic tile, consider the specific needs of your project, the level of foot traffic, and the desired aesthetic to make an informed decision. Read More

Benefits of Porcelain Tiles for Bathrooms
Water Resistance: Porcelain tiles are inherently water-resistant, making them ideal for humid and moisture-prone areas like bathrooms. They are impervious to water penetration, preventing damage and mold growth.
Durability: Porcelain tiles are durable and long-lasting, able to withstand heavy foot traffic, impact, and wear. They are also resistant to scratches, stains, and chemical damage, ensuring a low-maintenance surface.
Versatility: Available in a wide range of colors, patterns, sizes, and finishes, porcelain tiles offer endless design possibilities for bathroom floors, walls, shower enclosures, and backsplashes.

What is Porcelain Tile?
Porcelain tiles have become an increasingly popular choice in the world of interior design and construction, thanks to their exceptional durability, versatility, and timeless aesthetic appeal. As a leading porcelain tile company in the UK, it’s important for us to help our customers understand the unique qualities that make porcelain tiles such a smart and stylish option.
Porcelain tile is a type of ceramic tile made from finely ground clay minerals such as kaolinite, combined with other materials including feldspar, quartz, and carefully selected pigments. These raw materials are blended into a homogeneous mixture, which is then shaped into tiles through processes like extrusion or pressing.
What truly sets porcelain tiles apart is their high-temperature firing process — typically over 2100°F (1150°C). This intense heat transforms the clay and minerals into a vitrified, glass-like material, giving the tiles their renowned strength, density, and resistance to wear.

One of the standout benefits of porcelain tile is its impressive durability. Thanks to its dense structure and rigorous firing process, it’s highly resistant to cracks, scratches, and general wear and tear — making it perfect for use in homes, offices, and high-traffic areas.
Porcelain tiles also absorb far less water than standard ceramic tiles due to their low porosity. This makes them highly resistant to stains, moisture, and frost, making them ideal for both indoor and outdoor use in a variety of settings.

This property makes them highly resistant to water damage, making them suitable for areas exposed to moisture, such as bathrooms, kitchens, and outdoor spaces. Porcelain tiles are also less prone to freeze-thaw damage, making them an excellent choice for outdoor applications in colder climates.
Ceramic Tiles: Ceramic tiles have a higher water absorption rate, usually around 3% to 7%. While they are still suitable for most indoor applications, they may not be the best choice for areas with high humidity or direct water exposure.
Design Options:
Porcelain Tiles: Porcelain tiles offer a wide range of design options, including various colors, patterns, and textures. Modern manufacturing techniques can even mimic the appearance of natural materials like stone or wood, providing versatile options for both classic and contemporary designs.
Ceramic Tiles: Similar to porcelain tiles, ceramic tiles come in a variety of designs. However, the options may be more limited when compared to porcelain. Ceramic tiles are available in an array of colors and patterns, offering ample opportunities to personalize your space.
The differences between porcelain tiles and ceramic tiles lie in their composition, durability, water absorption, and design options. While both types of tiles have their merits, porcelain tiles, with their superior strength, low water absorption, and wide range of design choices, are often the preferred choice for high-traffic areas, bathrooms, kitchens, and outdoor applications.

How to Clean and Maintain Your Porcelain Tiles for Long-Lasting Beauty
As a proud owner of porcelain tiles, you know that they bring elegance and durability to your home. To keep them looking their best and to preserve their pristine beauty for years to come, proper cleaning and maintenance are essential. In this blog, we'll guide you How to Clean and Maintain Your Porcelain Tiles and offer valuable tips to ensure they stand the test of time.
1. Understanding Porcelain Tiles
Before diving into cleaning and maintenance, let's take a moment to understand what porcelain tiles are. Porcelain tiles are made from finely ground clay and other natural materials, kiln-fired at high temperatures, making them incredibly dense and water-resistant. These qualities make them ideal for high-traffic areas like kitchens and bathrooms.
2. Regular Sweeping and Dusting
One of the simplest yet most effective ways to maintain your porcelain tiles is through regular sweeping and dusting. Dust, dirt, and debris can accumulate on the surface, leading to potential scratching. Using a soft broom or a microfiber dust mop, sweep the floor regularly to keep it clean and prevent any abrasive particles from damaging the tiles.
3. Mopping with Warm Water
For routine cleaning, warm water alone can do wonders. Avoid using harsh chemicals as they might strip away the protective glaze on the tiles. Instead, dampen a mop or cloth with warm water and gently clean the porcelain surface. Dry the area thoroughly afterward to prevent water spots.
4. Addressing Spills and Stains Promptly
Accidents happen, and spills are inevitable. When a spill occurs, it's crucial to act quickly to prevent staining. Use a soft cloth or paper towel to blot the spill gently. Avoid rubbing the stain, as it can spread and become more difficult to remove. If needed, you can use a mild pH-balanced cleaner specifically formulated for porcelain tiles.
5. Dealing with Tough Stains
Some stains may be more stubborn and require a bit more effort to remove. For such stains, consider creating a paste with baking soda and water. Apply the paste to the stain, let it sit for a few minutes, and then scrub gently with a soft brush. Rinse the area thoroughly with warm water and wipe it dry.
6. Avoiding Abrasive Cleaners and Tools
As much as you may be tempted to use abrasive cleaners or harsh scrubbing tools, resist the urge! Abrasive cleaners and scrub brushes can scratch the glaze and damage the tiles' surface. Stick to soft cloths, microfiber mops, and non-abrasive cleaning solutions to protect your porcelain tiles.
7. Using Mats and Rugs
Prevention is key when it comes to maintaining your porcelain tiles. Placing mats or rugs at entryways can help trap dirt and grit from shoes, reducing the amount of debris that makes its way onto the tiles. Be sure to use mats with non-slip backings to prevent any accidents.
8. Being Cautious with Heavy Furniture
While porcelain tiles are incredibly durable, heavy furniture can still cause damage, especially if it is dragged across the floor. To protect your tiles, place felt pads under the legs of furniture to prevent scratching when moving them.
9. Regular Grout Maintenance
Don't forget about the grout lines! Regularly inspect the grout for any signs of wear, cracking, or discoloration. Clean the grout lines with a mild grout cleaner or a mixture of baking soda and water. Sealing the grout every year can also help maintain its appearance and prevent stains.
10. Seasonal Deep Cleaning
Every few months, consider giving your porcelain tiles a thorough deep cleaning. Use a pH-balanced, non-abrasive cleaner designed for porcelain tiles and follow the manufacturer's instructions. This deep clean will remove any hidden dirt or grime, leaving your tiles looking fresh and beautiful.
11. Professional Cleaning and Inspection
If you have stubborn stains or are uncertain about the best cleaning methods for your tiles, it's always a good idea to consult with a professional tile cleaner. They can provide expert advice and ensure your porcelain tiles receive the best care possible.
By following these maintenance tips, your wall tiles, floor tiles, kitchen tiles, bathroom tiles, & outdoor tiles will retain their beauty and durability, adding value and charm to your home for many years to come. Proper cleaning and care will not only keep your tiles looking fantastic but will also protect your investment, making them a worthy addition to any UK home. Global events often have a direct impact on the construction industry, and the ongoing conflict between the USA and Iran is no exception. The disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has created uncertainty in global shipping, increased energy costs, and affected manufacturers around the world.
At Surfaces Tiles, we import porcelain tiles primarily from Spain and India. With offices in both countries, we are in regular contact with manufacturers, shipping companies and industry partners, allowing us to closely monitor market conditions and understand how these events are affecting the tile industry.
One of the biggest challenges has been the sharp increase in natural gas prices. Gas is one of the most important components in the production of porcelain tiles, as it is used to fire the tiles at extremely high temperatures. Reports from our manufacturing partners indicate that gas prices increased by around 80% in India and 20% in Spain, putting significant pressure on production costs.
The Indian tile industry was forced to suspend production for approximately one month during April 2027 due to gas shortages and rising costs. Production has now resumed, although manufacturers are operating with revised pricing to reflect the higher manufacturing expenses.
Shipping has also been affected. Based on discussions with shipping lines and information currently available, ocean freight rates are expected to remain above normal levels for at least the next six months. Once freight markets stabilise, we expect some reduction in overall tile costs, but this is unlikely to happen immediately.
Despite these global challenges, the UK tile market has remained relatively stable compared with many other parts of the world. Since a large proportion of tiles supplied to the UK come from Spain, price increases have been more moderate than in some other markets.
As suppliers to homeowners, builders and construction companies across the UK and Ireland, we speak with our customers every day. While building material costs have increased across almost every category, we have not seen major construction companies delaying or cancelling their tile purchases. This gives us confidence that demand within the UK market remains healthy.
At Surfaces Tiles, we have not increased our selling prices during the past year, and at present we have no plans to do so. We believe the current situation is temporary and expect costs to improve once global shipping and energy markets become more stable. Rather than passing every increase directly to our customers, we have chosen to absorb much of the additional cost within our own margins.
Our advice to homeowners and trade professionals is simple: if your project is ready to proceed, there is little reason to delay purely because of tile prices. The second thing to keep in mind is never mix two colours in your bathroom. It will make the bathroom space busier and eventually it will look smaller in size. Instead of that use the same colour highlighter with punch effect on it. If possible, use the liner punch at the level of your eyesight, approximately at the height of 4 to 6 feet from the floor.  With this combination you can also select the 60x60 cm tiles if your space is not allowing you to use the 60x120 cm tiles.
The second option is to use some vibrant and dark colours with very small-size tiles, often called subway tiles. I know I am contradicting my previous statement that use light and soft colour in the smaller size bathrooms. But here I am suggesting darker shades with a major change in the size of the tile when you are using dark colours like black, dark grey, deep blue or bottle green colour for your bathroom. Keep the finish of the tile matt of soft matt and do not use glossy tile in subway sizes as well. Glossy finish is more popular in subway tiles, but we suggest them only for the kitchen application and not for the bathroom application.
Lastly, the bathroom Accessories place a major role in smaller size bathrooms. These are the things which will provide the luxurious look to your bathroom. Try to use the slightly contrast bathroom accessories from your tiles and do not select glossy finish in the bathroom accessories as well. Try to use the matt finish accessories. Always use the LED mirrors with back lighting. It will give a proper look to your bathroom.
